```{r}
#| label: setup
source("functions.R")
pop <- populations$cauchy
```

# 1. What population are you sampling from?

The Cauchy distribution with location 0 and scale 1 has density f(x) = 1 / (π (1 + x²)). One way to picture it: a
lighthouse 1 km off a straight coast spins and flashes at a random angle; the point on the coast where the beam hits is
Cauchy distributed. Most hits are near the point straight ahead, but when the beam is almost parallel to the coast it
lands extremely far away.

Near the center it looks like a bell curve: it is symmetric, its median is 0, and its quartiles are −1 and 1 (so its
interquartile range, IQR, is 2). But its tails are so heavy that the mean and the variance do not exist: the integrals
that define them do not converge. So the third CLT assumption, a finite variance, fails. The draws are still
independent and identically distributed.

```{r}
#| label: population
#| fig.width: 7
#| fig.height: 4.5
set.seed(student_id)
popDraws <- pop$generator(100000)

hist(popDraws[abs(popDraws) < 10], breaks = 80, probability = TRUE, col = "gray85", border = "white",
     main = "Cauchy(0, 1) population (values between -10 and 10)", xlab = "Individual value")
curve(dcauchy(x) / (2 / pi * atan(10)), add = TRUE, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
curve(dnorm(x), add = TRUE, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("Cauchy(0, 1) density (within -10 to 10)", "N(0, 1) density"),
       col = c("firebrick", "steelblue"), lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")

data.frame(
  quantity = c("lower quartile", "median", "upper quartile", "share beyond +/- 10", "largest |value|"),
  theoretical = c(-1, 0, 1, 1 - 2 / pi * atan(10), Inf),
  simulated = c(quantile(popDraws, 0.25), median(popDraws), quantile(popDraws, 0.75),
                mean(abs(popDraws) > 10), max(abs(popDraws)))
)
```

The quartiles and the median match the theory. The histogram only shows values between −10 and 10 (so I scaled the
red Cauchy curve to that window), because
`r round(100 * mean(abs(popDraws) > 10), 1)` percent of the draws are further out, and the largest one is `r format(round(max(abs(popDraws))), big.mark = ",")` away from 0.

How heavy are the tails? I compared the chance of a value further than k from 0 with a standard normal.

```{r}
#| label: tailCompare
k <- c(2, 3, 5, 10, 100)
tailCompare <- data.frame(
  k = k,
  cauchy = 1 - 2 / pi * atan(k),
  normal = 2 * (1 - pnorm(k))
)
knitr::kable(signif(tailCompare, 3))
```

A Cauchy value is further than 3 from the center `r round(100 * tailCompare$cauchy[k == 3], 1)` percent of the time, compared with
`r round(100 * tailCompare$normal[k == 3], 2)` percent for a normal, and it is further than 100 about `r round(100 * tailCompare$cauchy[k == 100], 2)` percent of the time, which
a normal value essentially never is.

# 2. What did you expect before running the simulation?

In 02die.qmd, 03exponential.qmd and 04binomial.qmd the sampling distribution of the mean moved closer to a normal
distribution as n grew. The Cauchy breaks one of the CLT assumptions, so I expected a completely different result.

## The sample mean: no n works

The Cauchy has tails so heavy that its mean and variance do not exist. The draws are still independent and identically
distributed, but the CLT also needs a finite variance, and that assumption fails. From this I expected:

* The shape never changes. A known result is that the mean of n independent Cauchy(0, 1) values is again
  Cauchy(0, 1). So the distribution of the sample mean should not get any narrower, and it should look the same at
  n = 1 and at n = 3,000.
* The spread and the tail share stay fixed. With no population variance, the formula sigma / sqrt(n) does not work.
  The IQR of the sample means should stay at the theoretical value of 2 however large n is, and the chance that a
  sample mean is further than 10 from 0 should stay at 1 − (2 / π) arctan(10) ≈ `r round(100 * (1 - 2 / pi * atan(10)), 1)` percent for every n.
* My checks break down. Because the theoretical moments do not exist, the simulated SD, skewness and kurtosis of the
  sample means should not settle on any value; they should jump around each time an extreme value appears.
* The QQ plot and the running mean never settle. In 02die.qmd the share of each face moved steadily toward 1/6 as the
  rolls came in. For the Cauchy I expected the running mean of one long sequence to keep jumping, because a single
  huge value can pull the whole average, and I expected the QQ plot to stay far off the line at both ends at every n.

So for the sample mean I expected that no n would work.

## The sample median: should become normal

Unlike the mean, the sample median is not affected by the extreme values in the tails; how much it varies depends on
the density near the center of the distribution. A known large sample result for sample quantiles (similar in spirit to
the CLT) says the median becomes approximately normal as n grows, with standard error

$$\text{SE(median)} \approx \frac{1}{2 f(0) \sqrt{n}}.$$

For the standard Cauchy the density at the center is f(0) = 1 / π = `r round(dcauchy(0), 3)`, so the SE should be about π / (2 sqrt(n)) and
shrink as n grows (for example `r round(pi / (2 * sqrt(100)), 3)` at n = 100).

I had no formula for the n at which the median would pass my standard. The Cauchy has very heavy tails, but it is
perfectly symmetric, and in 02die.qmd a symmetric population became normal quickly. So I expected the median to become
normal fairly fast, and borrowing the usual rule of thumb, I guessed somewhere between n = 30 and n = 40.

In short: the sample mean should never pass my normality checks however large n is, but the sample median should pass
the QQ correlation, skewness and kurtosis checks from some n on.

# 3. Which sample sizes did you investigate?

## The sample mean

Because I expected the answer "never", I chose a grid that goes far beyond the usual range, up to n = 3,000:
`r paste(pop$coarse, collapse = ", ")`. If even n = 3,000 does not help, a larger n will not either.

```{r}
#| label: simulate
res <- analyzePopulation(pop)
tab <- res$table
nStar <- smallestN(tab)
showTable(tab)
```

The columns seRatio, theoMean and predSkew are empty (NA) because the theoretical mean, SD and skewness do not exist.
The sample SD, skewness and kurtosis are numbers that can always be computed, but they jump around: the SD of the
means ranged from `r round(min(tab$simSD))` to `r format(round(max(tab$simSD)), big.mark = ",")`, the skewness from `r round(min(tab$skew))` to `r round(max(tab$skew))`. No n passed my checks.

Since the moments do not exist, I also looked at summaries that do exist for a Cauchy distribution: the median, the
quartiles, and the share of means beyond ±10.

```{r}
#| label: robust
robust <- data.frame(
  n = tab$n,
  medianOfMeans = sapply(res$means, median),
  lowerQuartile = sapply(res$means, function(m) quantile(m, 0.25)),
  upperQuartile = sapply(res$means, function(m) quantile(m, 0.75)),
  iqrOfMeans = sapply(res$means, IQR),
  shareBeyond10 = sapply(res$means, function(m) mean(abs(m) > 10)),
  largestAbsMean = sapply(res$means, function(m) max(abs(m)))
)
knitr::kable(robust, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

## The sample median

To check my prediction about the median, I ran the same search with the sample median instead of the mean. The
theoretical standard error here is the large n formula π / (2 sqrt(n)).

```{r}
#| label: medianSearch
medianRes <- searchN(NULL, c(1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, 200, 300), mu = 0,
                     theoSE = function(n) pi / (2 * sqrt(n)),
                     pred = function(n) c(skew = NA, kurt = NA),
                     meansFun = function(n, reps) replicate(reps, median(rcauchy(n))))
medianTab <- medianRes$table
medianN <- smallestN(medianTab)
knitr::kable(medianTab[, c("n", "simMean", "simSD", "theoSE", "seRatio", "skew", "exKurt", "qqCor", "normalEnough")],
             digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
```

# 4. When did the sampling distribution become approximately normal?

$$\boxed{\text{No } n \text{ works for the sample mean}}$$

```{r}
#| label: summaryNumbers
iqrRange <- range(robust$iqrOfMeans)
qqRange <- range(tab$qqCor)
beyondRange <- range(robust$shareBeyond10)
medianStar <- medianTab[medianTab$n == medianN, ]
```

The sample mean never became approximately normal: at every n from 1 to 3,000 its IQR stayed between
`r round(iqrRange[1], 2)` and `r round(iqrRange[2], 2)`, the value 2 of a single Cauchy draw, and its QQ correlation stayed between `r round(qqRange[1], 3)` and
`r round(qqRange[2], 3)`, far below my cutoff of `r criteria$qqCor`. The sample median, on the other hand, became approximately normal at
n = `r medianN`.

```{r}
#| label: whyNoN
#| fig.width: 10
#| fig.height: 5
nAll <- sort(unique(c(tab$n, medianTab$n)))
plot(NULL, xlim = range(nAll), ylim = c(0.01, 5), log = "xy",
     xlab = "Sample size n (log scale)", ylab = "IQR (log scale)",
     main = "The spread of the mean never shrinks; the spread of the median does")
lines(robust$n, robust$iqrOfMeans, type = "o", pch = 16, lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
lines(medianTab$n, sapply(medianRes$means, IQR), type = "o", pch = 16, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")
nLine <- exp(seq(log(1), log(3000), length.out = 200))
lines(nLine, 2 * qnorm(0.75) * pi / (2 * sqrt(nLine)), lty = 2, col = "steelblue")
abline(h = 2, lty = 2, col = "firebrick")
legend("bottomleft", c("IQR of the sample means", "IQR = 2 (one Cauchy draw)", "IQR of the sample medians",
                       "Normal theory for the median"),
       col = c("firebrick", "firebrick", "steelblue", "steelblue"), lty = c(1, 2, 1, 2), pch = c(16, NA, 16, NA),
       lwd = c(2, 1, 2, 1), bty = "n")
```

How to read it: if averaging helped, the red line would fall like the blue one. Instead it stays flat at 2 for every n.
The dashed blue line is the IQR a normal distribution with SE π / (2 sqrt(n)) would have; the medians follow it once n
is not small.

# 5. How do the simulated mean and standard error compare with theory?

There is no theoretical mean or standard error to compare with, so the usual comparison is impossible. What I can
compare is the behaviour:

* The median of the sample means stayed between `r round(min(robust$medianOfMeans), 3)` and `r round(max(robust$medianOfMeans), 3)`, close to the center 0, but the
  average of the 10,000 sample means (simMean) ranged from `r round(min(tab$simMean), 2)` to `r round(max(tab$simMean), 2)` and does not settle on any value.
* The SD of the sample means did not shrink like 1 / sqrt(n). It was `r round(tab$simSD[tab$n == 1])` at n = 1 and `r round(tab$simSD[tab$n == 3000])` at
  n = 3,000, with values as large as `r format(round(max(tab$simSD)), big.mark = ",")` in between, set by single extreme draws.

```{r}
#| label: runningMean
#| fig.width: 9
#| fig.height: 4.5
runningMean <- cumsum(popDraws) / seq_along(popDraws)
plot(runningMean, type = "l", log = "x", xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Number of draws (log scale)", ylab = "Running mean",
     main = paste0("Running mean of 100,000 Cauchy draws (seed ", student_id, ")"))
axis(1, at = c(1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000), labels = c("1", "10", "100", "1,000", "10,000", "100,000"))
abline(h = 0, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)
jumpAt <- which.max(abs(diff(runningMean)))
lateJump <- 10000 + which.max(abs(diff(runningMean))[-(1:10000)])
```

The running mean of one long sequence does not settle down. The largest single jump happened at draw
`r format(jumpAt + 1, big.mark = ",")`, where one value of `r format(round(popDraws[jumpAt + 1]), big.mark = ",")` moved the mean of all draws so far from
`r round(runningMean[jumpAt], 2)` to `r round(runningMean[jumpAt + 1], 2)`. Even after 10,000 draws the mean still jumped: the largest jump after draw
10,000 was at draw `r format(lateJump + 1, big.mark = ",")`, by `r round(abs(diff(runningMean))[lateJump], 2)`. For a population with a finite mean, this curve would flatten out (as the
shares of a die did in 02die.qmd).

# 6. Why did you choose that value?

```{r}
#| label: samplingPlots
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 6
old <- par(mfrow = c(2, 4), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (n in c(1, 30, 1000, 3000)) {
  m <- res$means[[as.character(n)]]
  hist(m[abs(m) < 10], breaks = 60, probability = TRUE, col = "gray85", border = "white",
       main = paste0("Sample means, n = ", n), xlab = "Sample mean (between -10 and 10)", ylim = c(0, 0.4))
  curve(dcauchy(x) / (2 / pi * atan(10)), add = TRUE, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
}
for (n in c(1, 30, 1000, 3000)) {
  m <- res$means[[as.character(n)]]
  qqnorm(m, main = paste("QQ plot: n =", n), pch = 16, cex = 0.3)
  qqline(m, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
}
par(old)
```

The red curve is the same Cauchy(0, 1) density (scaled to the window from −10 to 10) in every panel, and the histograms follow it at n = 1, 30, 1,000 and
3,000 alike. The QQ plots are flat in the middle and shoot off at both ends at every n: most means are near 0, and a
few are enormous.

I concluded that no n works for the sample mean because:

* The IQR of the means stayed at about 2 at every n, so the spread did not shrink at all, as predicted by the exact
  result that the mean of n Cauchy values is again Cauchy(0, 1).
* The share of means beyond ±10 stayed between `r round(100 * beyondRange[1], 1)` and `r round(100 * beyondRange[2], 1)` percent at every n, close to the predicted
  `r round(100 * (1 - 2 / pi * atan(10)), 1)` percent, so the heavy tails did not thin out.
* The QQ correlation never came close to my cutoff, and it did not improve with n.
* Going up to n = 3,000 made no difference, so a larger n would not help either.

The reason is the heavy tail. A single draw can be so large that it outweighs all the others: the largest absolute
sample mean at n = 100 was `r format(round(robust$largestAbsMean[robust$n == 100]), big.mark = ",")`. When one value can dominate a sum, averaging cannot cancel it out.

# 7. What surprised you?

```{r}
#| label: predictionCheck
predictionCheck <- data.frame(
  Prediction = c(
    "IQR of the means stays at 2 for every n",
    "QQ correlation stays far below the cutoff at every n",
    "SD, skewness and kurtosis of the means jump around",
    paste0("Share beyond +/- 10 stays at about ", round(100 * (1 - 2 / pi * atan(10)), 1), " percent"),
    "Running mean never settles",
    "No n works for the mean",
    "The median becomes normal at about n = 30 to 40"
  ),
  Result = c(
    paste0("IQR between ", round(iqrRange[1], 2), " and ", round(iqrRange[2], 2)),
    paste0("QQ correlation between ", round(qqRange[1], 3), " and ", round(qqRange[2], 3)),
    paste0("SD from ", round(min(tab$simSD)), " to ", format(round(max(tab$simSD)), big.mark = ",")),
    paste0(round(100 * beyondRange[1], 1), " to ", round(100 * beyondRange[2], 1), " percent"),
    "Large jumps even after many thousands of draws",
    paste("No tested n passed; smallestN gives", nStar),
    paste("Median passed from n =", medianN)
  ),
  Match = c("Same", "Same", "Same", "Same", "Same", "Same",
            ifelse(medianN >= 30 & medianN <= 40, "Same", "Different"))
)
knitr::kable(predictionCheck)
```

Every prediction about the mean held, which is not surprising, because they follow from an exact mathematical result.
What still surprised me was how complete the failure looks. Knowing the result is different from seeing it: the
histogram at n = 3,000 is the same as the histogram at n = 1. Collecting 3,000 times more data did not make the
average any more precise, because the chance that one draw is large enough to move the mean by a given amount does
not shrink as n grows.

The second surprise was the median. Using the same population and the same standard, the median became approximately
normal at n = `r medianN` (skewness `r round(medianStar$skew, 3)`, excess kurtosis `r round(medianStar$exKurt, 3)`, QQ correlation `r round(medianStar$qqCor, 4)`), and its SD
was close to π / (2 sqrt(n)) (ratio `r round(medianStar$seRatio, 3)` at n = `r medianN`). So the problem is not that Cauchy data are useless; it is
that the mean is the wrong summary for them. It did take longer than my guess of 30 to 40. The last check to pass was
the kurtosis, not the skewness: the median is symmetric, as I expected, but its distribution has slightly heavier
tails than a normal one for small n, and its excess kurtosis stayed a little above `r criteria$kurt` until about n = 50
(`r round(medianTab$exKurt[medianTab$n == 30], 3)` at n = 30 and `r round(medianTab$exKurt[medianTab$n == 48], 3)` at n = 48). The symmetry made the skewness pass early, but symmetry says nothing
about the kurtosis. Also, n = 45 passed once by luck before n = 46 and 48 failed again.

Compared with my other populations, the Cauchy is the only one where the answer is not a number. For the die,
the exponential and the binomial, the CLT worked and only the speed was different; here a CLT assumption is broken
and no amount of data fixes it.

## Limitations

* "No n works" is a mathematical fact for the Cauchy mean; my simulation only illustrates it up to n = 3,000 with one
  seed. It cannot prove anything about larger n on its own.
* My usual checks (skewness, kurtosis, SE ratio) describe moments that do not exist here, so for the mean I relied
  on the IQR, quartiles and tail shares instead.
* The histograms only show sample means between −10 and 10, so they hide the extreme values; the QQ plots and
  the table show them.
* The theoretical SE of the median, π / (2 sqrt(n)), is a large n formula, so the SE ratio for the median is only
  meaningful once n is not small.
* All rows come from one random stream (seed `r student_id`), so they are not independent of each other.
